title: Voice Memo on Quitting the Optimization of My Own Body
script: Narrator: [wry] Recording this after deleting the sleep app, the macro tracker, and the recovery ring app, all in the same restless hour, which feels almost ceremonial in retrospect.
Narrator: [reflective] For three years I treated my body as a project requiring perpetual optimization, as though wellness were a metric that could be perfected rather than simply inhabited.
Narrator: [honest] Every meal became data before it became nourishment. Every walk was logged before it was actually enjoyed, if enjoyment even remained the point anymore.

Narrator: [thoughtful] What finally cracked the illusion was noticing how anxious I felt on days the numbers disappointed me, an anxiety wildly disproportionate to whatever the number actually measured.
Narrator: [wry] A single night of poor sleep score, and I'd narrate the entire following day as compromised, regardless of how I actually felt moving through it.

Narrator: [analytical] I'd essentially outsourced the authority to interpret my own body to a wearable device manufactured by a company with no interest in my actual wellbeing, only my continued subscription.
Narrator: [honest] The language of optimization, I've come to suspect, quietly imports the logic of productivity into a domain that was never meant to operate that way.
Narrator: [reflective] Bodies aren't machines awaiting efficiency gains; they're something closer to weather, responsive to forces far beyond whatever a dashboard claims to capture.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Deleting the apps felt, absurdly, like a small act of rebellion, though rebellion against what, exactly, I'm still working out.
Narrator: [uncertain] The first week without them was disorienting, an itch to check numbers that no longer existed to check, muscle memory searching for data that had vanished.
Narrator: [warmly] Gradually, though, I noticed myself asking simpler questions instead: am I hungry, am I tired, do I want to move, questions a device had quietly been answering for me.

Narrator: [peacefully] I don't know yet whether this experiment will last permanently, but for now, inhabiting my body has started to feel less like managing a portfolio and more like simply living in it.
